item.text: I’ll read all five parts in order, map each new note to the existing questions or new ones, then write the JSONL and run the required check.

item.aggregated_output:
<<2:283 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
2:283/q01 What does safar mean and evoke? [سَفَرٍۢ · meaning]
  2:283/q01/p1 Travel, whose root conveys uncovering or disclosure. — reasons: Wahidi cites travel exposing character, the book making clear, dawn, uncovering a face, reconciliation, sweeping, and Ibn al-Aʿrabi's al-Akhtal line; al-Azhari says the traveler emerges into open country and cites daylight and Sirius; Razi repeats these cognates.
2:283/q02 How does 'on a journey' work in the sentence? [عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ · grammar]
  2:283/q02/p1 It means being in the state of travel; ʿalā evokes firm establishment in it. — reasons: Abu Hayyan glosses the phrase 'while traveling'; Alusi calls it a dependent metaphor and allows coordination or a circumstantial reading.
2:283/q03 Why mention travel here? [عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the conditional describes a typical obstacle or limits lawful pledging.)
  2:283/q03/p1 Travel is the common setting where writing or witnesses are unavailable; comparable obstacles also call for security. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Elmalılı and Ibn Ashur cite scarcity of scribes, tools, witnesses, night, busyness, or doubtful debtor standing. Burhan notes a conditional need not be legally restrictive. Razi compares the fear clause in 4:101.
  2:283/q03/p2 The travel condition is restrictive for pledges. — reasons: Mujahid, Dahhak and Dawud follow the apparent conditional wording; Dahhak also requires absence of a scribe. Tabari rejects its restriction on pledges by the armor report, while others reject it as customary context.
2:283/q04 What is read and meant by 'a scribe'? [كَاتِبًۭا · readings] (turns on: Whether the absent resource is a writer, writing materials, or written documents, and how the consonantal text is read.)
  2:283/q04/p1 Kitāban, writing or writing materials, including pen, ink and paper. — reasons: Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid and Abu al-Aliya say a writer may be present without materials; Tabari records variant specific lacks of ink, paper, or writer. Nahhas calls it anomalous; Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi find its sense apt despite codex spelling.
  2:283/q04/p2 Kātiban, a single writer. — reasons: Tabari prefers the codex and regional reading; Nahhas relates it to 2:282's 'let a writer write'; Thalabi cites the majority and codex. Other sources note the common reading.
  2:283/q04/p3 Kuttāban or kitāban as plural writers. — reasons: Dahhak reads a plural of 'writer'; Nahhas says kitāb can be a collective of scribes; Ibn Abbas reasons each case has a scribe.
  2:283/q04/p4 Kutuban, written books or records. — reasons: Abu al-Aliya's plural of kitāb fits multiple cases.
2:283/q05 How is 'you do not find a scribe' attached syntactically? [وَلَمْ تَجِدُوا۟ كَاتِبًۭا · grammar]
  2:283/q05/p1 It may coordinate with the condition, attach to kāna's predicate, or be a circumstantial clause. — reasons: Samin distinguishes the latter two as nominative-context constructions; Abu Hayyan also lists attachments.
2:283/q06 What is a rahn or pledged security? [فَرِهَٰنٌۭ · meaning]
  2:283/q06/p1 An item retained or delivered as security for a debt; the root also conveys permanence, detention or firmness. — reasons: Wahidi and Razi explain transfer from verbal noun to object name; Qurtubi says it is recoverable by sale proceeds. Ibn Ashur adduces 74:38 and Zuhayr; Farisi cites Abu Zayd and 66:12; poetry in Aʿsha and others shows pledged property, persons and enduring food.
2:283/q07 Do rahana and arhana differ in use? [فَرِهَٰنٌۭ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the two verbs are interchangeable in collateral usage and whether arhana carries a separate bidding sense.)
  2:283/q07/p1 Both can mean to pledge collateral. — reasons: Zajjaj, Ibn al-Aʿrabi and al-Akhfash allow both; poetry attributed to Ibn Hammam is adduced, but al-Asmaʿi disputes its wording. Wahidi, Qurtubi, Samin and Tabrisi record the disagreement.
  2:283/q07/p2 Rahana is standard for pledging, while arhana may mean outbidding, giving another's pledge, or keeping something going. — reasons: Abu Ali and Abu Zayd distinguish loans and sales from bidding high; Farra gives another-person sense; Ibn Atiyya and Samin cite the high-price camel, and rahantu lisani excludes arhana.
2:283/q08 How is 'pledges' read and formed? [فَرِهَٰنٌۭ · readings] (turns on: The transmitted vowels and alif, the regularity of their plural patterns, codex spelling, and usage in horse racing.)
  2:283/q08/p1 Ruhun, with two dammas and no alif, is a transmitted plural of rahn. — reasons: Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it, with Ibn Abbas, Ubayy's transmission, and others; some analyze it like rare suquf. Zajjaj prefers it for codex fit and valid transmission. Abu Amr distinguishes ordinary pledges from rihān for horse wagers; poetry supports rahn.
  2:283/q08/p2 Rihān, with kasra and alif, is the regular plural of rahn. — reasons: Most readers use it; Akhfash, Tabari, Nahhas, Razi and Samin favor its productive pattern such as hibal from habl. Sibawayh's caution weighs against invented plurals of plurals; Qiraat-ER also calls it canonical.
  2:283/q08/p3 Ruhn, with a still hāʾ, is a lightened form of ruhun. — reasons: Reports assign it to Ikrima, Asim, Meccans or particular Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr transmissions; Nahhas explains dropping ḍamma for weight and prefers an adjectival analogy; Akhfash criticizes the rare pattern. Thalabi treats vowelled and unvowelled forms as dialect variants.
2:283/q09 How does 'pledges held' function grammatically? [فَرِهَٰنٌۭ مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · grammar] (turns on: The omitted clause element and whether rahn functions as object noun or verbal noun.)
  2:283/q09/p1 A nominative subject with omitted predicate, or predicate of an omitted subject such as 'the security'; an implied command to take one is also possible. — reasons: Jishumi allows nominative and imperative or accusative ellipses; Razi, Baydawi, Qurtubi's Mahdawi and Samin lay out the alternatives; Alusi treats it as security, a thing to take, or a prescription.
  2:283/q09/p2 The pledge noun is a lexicalized verbal noun used as an object, not a cognate accusative. — reasons: Farisi, Wahidi, Razi and Samin distinguish object usage from a verbal noun used adverbially; Ibn Atiyya says its noun status permits the plural with kasra.
2:283/q10 When may a pledge be taken? [عَلَىٰ سَفَرٍۢ فَرِهَٰنٌۭ · law] (turns on: Whether the travel and scribe conditions restrict the law or describe a typical need for security.)
  2:283/q10/p1 Pledges are valid during travel or residence, with or without an available scribe. — reasons: The Prophet pledged armor to a Jewish seller in Medina; reports differ over twenty or thirty measures of barley and the seller's name. Majority jurists treat travel as an example; Razi compares 4:101. Ibn Atiyya says the verse's general meaning itself extends to home.
  2:283/q10/p2 Only during travel, and for some authorities only if a writer is unavailable. — reasons: Mujahid, Dahhak and Dawud take the travel and lack-of-scribe conditions literally; Dahhak directs writing instead whenever possible.
  2:283/q10/p3 If writing is available, pledging is permissible but ordinarily not recommended without another reason. — reasons: Elmalılı distinguishes legal permission from prudent resort to collateral.
2:283/q11 What does qabḍ mean in 'held in possession'? [مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · meaning]
  2:283/q11/p1 Grasping and holding something in the palm. — reasons: Jishumi contrasts emphatic ḍād with qabṣ using un-emphatic ṣād, which means holding with the fingertips.
2:283/q12 What does possession do to a pledge's legal effect? [مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · law] (turns on: At what stage the contract binds, and whose physical custody satisfies maqbudah.)
  2:283/q12/p1 Taking possession is required for validity or binding completion; a mere verbal pledge has no operative security. — reasons: Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa treat possession as a condition of validity; many cite 'held.' Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some reports specify receipt by creditor. Ibn Atiyya says creditor or agent certainly counts, and Baghawi says the pledgor cannot reclaim collateral while debt remains.
  2:283/q12/p2 Malik treats offer and acceptance as a binding contract before delivery; possession completes its benefit and can be compelled. — reasons: Malikis invoke 5:1 and 17:34 and covenant fulfillment; reports distinguish validity, bindingness and usefulness. KuranYolu says valid but binding upon delivery, while other notes say already binding, a nuance in reporting.
2:283/q13 Whose custody counts as possession of a pledge? [مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · law] (turns on: Whether a proxy or neutral custodian counts as a valid holder.)
  2:283/q13/p1 Only creditor possession counts, not holding by a neutral third party. — reasons: Al-Hakam, Qatada, Ata, Ibn Abi Layla and a report from Ahmad require the creditor's own receipt.
  2:283/q13/p2 Possession by the creditor's agent suffices. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya reports consensus, and Alusi infers it from the passive maqbudah; Abu Hayyan agrees.
  2:283/q13/p3 A neutral custodian's possession counts. — reasons: Malik, his school and the majority treat the custodian as creditor's representative; Qurtubi says loss in the custodian's care creates no liability for creditor or trustee.
2:283/q14 What if a pledge returns to the debtor? [مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · law] (turns on: Whether renewed debtor custody undoes the security, and whether its legal form matters.)
  2:283/q14/p1 Return to the debtor voids the pledge. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya relates this to its defining held state; Qurtubi follows loss of possession. Abu Hayyan reports Malik says absolute return voids it.
  2:283/q14/p2 A loan or deposit back to the debtor preserves it. — reasons: Abu Hanifa makes this exception.
  2:283/q14/p3 Prior possession continues to count after return. — reasons: Qurtubi reports Shafi'i this way, but Abu Hayyan reports him as voiding it whenever returned; the reports conflict.
2:283/q15 Can debt

 claims or uncertain property be pledged? [رِهَٰنٌۭ مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · law] (turns on: Whether the collateral can be physically possessed and realized, especially for debt claims and common shares.)
  2:283/q15/p1 Only valuable, saleable and deliverable property; debts and uncertain property cannot be pledged. — reasons: The majority require realizable security and physical possession. A cited Razi argument excludes an undivided share because it cannot be physically received. KuranYolu bars human beings despite pre-Islamic child hostages.
  2:283/q15/p2 A debt or uncertain property can serve as collateral. — reasons: Malik permits debt claims and examples such as runaway slave, stray camel, fetus, fish and unripe fruit; Qurtubi argues anything saleable has value.
2:283/q16 Can an undivided share be pledged? [فَرِهَٰنٌۭ مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · law] (turns on: Whether an undivided share can be received as security.)
  2:283/q16/p1 An undivided share cannot be pledged. — reasons: Abu Hanifa and the argument cited by Razi and Elmalılı rely on inability to take definite possession.
  2:283/q16/p2 An undivided property share may be pledged. — reasons: Malik and Shafi'i allow divisible or indivisible shares; Ibn al-Mundhir compares sale and notes a Hanafi joint-creditor exception.
  2:283/q16/p3 An undivided share may be pledged only if it cannot be divided. — reasons: Al-Hasan ibn Salih's intermediate rule.
2:283/q17 Which growth of collateral remains pledged? [رِهَٰنٌۭ مَّقْبُوضَةٌۭ · law]
  2:283/q17/p1 The pledged property's inseparable growth follows the pledge, but separable fruits do not unless stipulated. — reasons: Qurtubi distinguishes fattening and offspring from crops, milk, wool and fruit, citing independent alms treatment of the latter.
2:283/q18 Does a secured creditor have priority over other creditors? [فَرِهَٰنٌۭ · law]
  2:283/q18/p1 The secured creditor has priority over other creditors. — reasons: Malik and many jurists give priority when the debtor has not already been declared insolvent; Qurtubi rejects a report of equal sharing.
2:283/q19 May the creditor use pledged property? [رِهَٰنٌۭ · law] (turns on: Who owns benefits, who pays upkeep, and whether maintenance or the contract permits creditor use.)
  2:283/q19/p1 Benefits belong to the owner, who bears upkeep; creditor use requires permission or is forbidden. — reasons: A report says the owner gets yield and bears loss. Malik, Shafi'i, Sha'bi and Ibn Sirin hold it; Khattabi prefers the explicit wording. Tahawi and Sha'bi argue the permissive report preceded the usury bar or was abrogated; Ibn Abd al-Barr reports agreement and warns of unknown benefit and usury.
  2:283/q19/p2 A creditor who feeds a pledged animal may ride it or drink its milk in proportion to upkeep. — reasons: A more explicit Abu Hurayra report is adopted by Ahmad and Ishaq; Abu Thawr, Awza'i and Layth permit analogous use when creditor maintained neglected collateral.
  2:283/q19/p3 A creditor may stipulate use in a sale or lease pledge, but not in a loan pledge. — reasons: Ibn Khuwayzimandad says use on a loan is interest.
2:283/q20 May a pledge become the creditor's property after nonpayment? [رِهَٰنٌۭ · law]
  2:283/q20/p1 No; pre-Islamic foreclosure at a deadline is barred. — reasons: Tabrisi, Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur cite the Prophetic 'the pledge is not foreclosed.' Qurtubi explains the indicative wording and disputed mursal chains; Zuhayr's verse recalls the earlier practice.
2:283/q21 What happened when the Prophet pledged his armor? [رِهَٰنٌۭ · reports]
  2:283/q21/p1 He pledged his armor to a Jewish seller for food on credit while in Medina. — reasons: Reports variously give twenty or thirty measures of barley, name Abu al-Shahm or leave the seller unnamed, and say the armor was still pledged at death. Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi recount his response that he was trustworthy.
2:283/q22 What does mutual trust permit in a debt transaction? [فَإِنْ أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضًۭا · law] (turns on: Whether the trust clause is a general independent option or a concession confined to inability to document.)
  2:283/q22/p1 The parties may omit writing, witnesses and collateral when they trust one another. — reasons: Sha'bi, Hasan and many exegetes take the clause as a general concession. Ibn Ashur extends it to each party and home or travel; Tabarisi sees evidence the safeguards are advisory.
  2:283/q22/p2 When documentation and witnesses are available, they must still be used; trust is a limited travel concession. — reasons: Tabari accepts a restriction on trust while rejecting restriction on pledges; Dahhak ties trust to travel and absence of a writer. Ibn Ashur finds Tabari's explanation unclear and suggests a traveler unable to pledge may rely on trust.
2:283/q23 Who trusts whom in the trust clause? [أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضًۭا · referent] (turns on: Whether the clause describes only reliance on the debtor or obligations on either party.)
  2:283/q23/p1 Ordinarily the creditor trusts the debtor with property or the debt. — reasons: Wahidi cites the language of security from betrayal and 8:11, 12:64; Ibn Ashur specifies lender and borrower. Biqai says the undefined parties could operate in either direction.
  2:283/q23/p2 Trust can run both ways between creditor and debtor. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says a debtor can trust a creditor holding collateral worth more than the debt; the creditor must return the excess faithfully. Biqai calls trust mutual.
2:283/q24 How is 'if some trust others' alternatively read? [فَإِنْ أَمِنَ بَعْضُكُم بَعْضًۭا · readings]
  2:283/q24/p1 Ubayy reads a passive, 'if some are trusted.' — reasons: Zamakhshari explains public confidence in the debtor; Samin treats baʿḍan as governed by a deleted preposition and an omitted property or debt complement. Sajaawandi reports an alternate reflexive form.
2:283/q25 Who is 'the one entrusted' and what must be given? [ٱلَّذِى ٱؤْتُمِنَ أَمَٰنَتَهُۥ · referent] (turns on: Whether the entrusted person is debtor, pledgee, or the party recording the debt.)
  2:283/q25/p1 The trusted debtor must repay the creditor's debt or property, without denial or delay. — reasons: Jishumi and Razi prefer this over pledgee. Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi cite consensus, judgments and reports. Tabari warns against absconding; Ibn Ashur includes returning the same thing or its equivalent. The name encourages faithful payment.
  2:283/q25/p2 The pledge holder must return collateral after the debt is paid. — reasons: Jishumi and Razi report this alternative because collateral itself is held in trust; Ibn Ashur includes a creditor holding an overvalued pledge as an entrusted party.
  2:283/q25/p3 The entrusted party must write the true sum without increase or decrease. — reasons: Zajjaj equates faithful rendering with justice in recording the obligation.
2:283/q26 What is meant by 'his trust' and whose is it? [أَمَٰنَتَهُۥ · meaning] (turns on: Whether amāna names the owed object or the fiduciary relation, and whether its pronoun belongs to creditor or debtor.)
  2:283/q26/p1 It is the debt or property owed, called a trust because security was waived. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Biqai and Alusi explain the nomenclature; the possessive may refer to debtor or creditor. Ibn Ashur says amāna can mean the object or quality of trust and compares a verbal noun joined to its object.
  2:283/q26/p2 It is the act or obligation of trust, with an omitted 'debt' or a charge to preserve honor by repayment. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya gives the honor nuance; Samin gives a verbal noun with omitted possessive and rejects using it as the verb's absolute object; Abu Hayyan lists both referents.
2:283/q27 How is 'entrusted' formed and pronounced? [ٱؤْتُمِنَ · grammar]
  2:283/q27/p1 It is an eighth-form passive from amāna with an original root hamza. — reasons: Akhfash and Nahhas explain the two hamzas and joining alif; Wāḥidī and Jishumi give the active and passive forms. At a fresh start the joining alif prevents two sounded hamzas.
2:283/q28 Which recitations of 'entrusted' are accepted? [ٱؤْتُمِنَ · readings] (turns on: Whether reported vowel gestures, letter substitution, assimilation and pause length fit transmission and Arabic phonology.)
  2:283/q28/p1 The usual connected reading retains a quiescent hamza after the joining hamza drops. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid, Farisi and Ibn Atiyya reject reported ḍamma indications as incorrect; Farisi argues the first radical of iftaʿala is still and vowel transfer goes backward. Ibn Ashur describes the majority pronunciation.
  2:283/q28/p2 A ḍamma-tinged or rounded hamza is transmitted from Asim, Hamza or Abu Bakr. — reasons: The transmission is described as ishām or a raised initial alif. Abu Ali defends Ahmad ibn Musa's account against Ibn Atiyya; other authorities reject the notation or performance.
  2:283/q28/p3 An assimilated itamin or attamin form is reported, but its acceptability is disputed. — reasons: Zamakhshari and Baydawi reject assimilation because the replacement letter retains hamza's status; Alusi cites Arabic usage, Aisha's speech and a Kufan grammatical defense.
  2:283/q28/p4 Warsh and others turn the hamza into a yāʾ-like sound in connected recitation. — reasons: Samin cites Warsh and Susi; Ibn Ashur explains an intermediary wāw from passive ḍamma followed by yāʾ after the linking hamza disappears. Baydawi accepts a yāʾ substitution.
  2:283/q28/p5 At a pause or initial pronunciation, substitute a matching vowel letter with shortening. — reasons: Samin explains the wāw-like onset; Ibn al-Jazari rejects restored madd or verified hamza, against Abu Shama's analogy; NASHR sets general rules for still hamza and competing madd causes.
2:283/q29 Why add 'fear God, his Lord'? [وَلْيَتَّقِ ٱللَّهَ رَبَّهُۥ · rhetoric]
  2:283/q29/p1 The doubled divine reference solemnly presses the debtor to repay and avoid betrayal. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says repeating God's name rather than a pronoun adds awe; Abu Hayyan no

tes 'his Lord' emphasizes piety at both acknowledgment and repayment; Alusi says human rights need guarding.
2:283/q30 Who is forbidden to conceal testimony? [وَلَا تَكْتُمُوا۟ ٱلشَّهَٰدَةَ · referent] (turns on: Whether the prohibition directly addresses transaction witnesses alone or also the debtor's acknowledgment.)
  2:283/q30/p1 Witnesses who know the transaction must disclose their testimony. — reasons: Tabari and early authorities address summoned witnesses; Jishumi includes those who attended the contract or pledge without formal appointment. Rabi insists even adverse evidence about self or kin is covered.
  2:283/q30/p2 Debtors too must acknowledge their own obligation rather than defeat testimony. — reasons: Baydawi allows debtors testifying against themselves, Elmalılı and Asad include a debtor denying an unsecured loan; Alusi rejects making debtors the primary addressee.
2:283/q31 When must testimony be offered? [وَلَا تَكْتُمُوا۟ ٱلشَّهَٰدَةَ · law] (turns on: Whether only a formal request triggers the duty, or known danger to a right calls for earlier disclosure.)
  2:283/q31/p1 When summoned or when a right risks loss, a witness must testify accurately; the duty may arise before being asked. — reasons: Tabari, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Atiyya speak of summons and risk; Qurtubi treats testimony as collective duty becoming individual for needed witnesses. Al-Qaffal and Ibn Ashur cite 'best witness before asked'; Ibn Ashur adds danger of death, absence or forgetting; KuranYolu reconciles reports criticizing unsolicited testimony as about false testimony or God's rights.
  2:283/q31/p2 One should avoid disclosing testimony in a venue where it will assist falsehood. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya qualifies Ibn Abbas's advice under corrupt conditions when ineffective disclosure may conceal the truth.
2:283/q32 What does concealing testimony mean? [وَلَا تَكْتُمُوا۟ ٱلشَّهَٰدَةَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether concealment is silence when evidence is needed or a false denial of knowledge.)
  2:283/q32/p1 Withholding known evidence, especially failing to speak when needed. — reasons: Jishumi contrasts kitmān with disclosure; Razi says refusal can defeat property rights. Ibn Ashur relates the recurring prohibition to 2:282.
  2:283/q32/p2 Denying that one knows of the event. — reasons: Razi cites the denial about Abraham's family in 2:140 as a parallel.
2:283/q33 How is the prohibition against concealment read? [وَلَا تَكْتُمُوا۟ · readings] (turns on: The opening consonant of the prohibitive verb and whether address remains direct.)
  2:283/q33/p1 Third-person plural, 'let them not conceal.' — reasons: Abu Abd al-Rahman and al-Sulami transmit yāʾ; Samin relates the form to the preceding scribe and witness, while noting a singular expression can mean a group.
  2:283/q33/p2 Second-person plural, directly addressing the hearers. — reasons: Jishumi calls this the apparent reading.
2:283/q34 What is the force of 'his heart is sinful'? [فَإِنَّهُۥٓ ءَاثِمٌۭ قَلْبُهُۥ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the phrase foregrounds a corrupt state of the heart or the sin incurred by this act.)
  2:283/q34/p1 The concealer's heart becomes guilty, wicked or corrupt; concealment is a grave sin. — reasons: Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Suddi and others call the heart wicked. Ibn Abbas ranks concealment with shirk and false testimony; Wahidi mentions a sealed, hypocritical heart. A Prophetic report equates it to false testimony. Elmalılı says it approaches unbelief.
  2:283/q34/p2 It states the heart has incurred the sin of suppressing testimony. — reasons: Mawardi's alternative and Ibn Atiyya stress the guilt attaching to the act.
2:283/q35 Why attribute sin to the heart? [ءَاثِمٌۭ قَلْبُهُۥ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether attribution is rhetorical causal language or grounds for a stronger claim that the heart is the acting subject.)
  2:283/q35/p1 Concealment begins in inward intention and knowledge, and the heart governs outward acts; naming it intensifies blame. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan cite the Prophetic sound-body morsel; Tabrisi cites 58:22; Qurtubi calls it part-for-whole; Ibn Ashur names perception, emotion and intention. Biqai and Bursevi link a corrupted heart to the body. Alusi rejects extra black-mark and body-effect theories.
  2:283/q35/p2 The heart itself is the acting and accountable subject. — reasons: Many theologians infer this from the verse and 26:193.
  2:283/q35/p3 The act can be attributed to an organ because it supplies the act's chief cause. — reasons: Opponents of the theological inference compare the eye seeing and ear hearing; Razi says bodily acts follow heart motives.
2:283/q36 How is 'āthim qalbuhu' parsed? [ءَاثِمٌۭ قَلْبُهُۥ · grammar] (turns on: The governing role of the active participle and whether definiteness permits a specification analysis.)
  2:283/q36/p1 Āthim is the predicate and qalbuhu its nominative agent or subject. — reasons: Nahhas lists this; Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Samin report it, and Abu Hayyan and Samin prefer it. It says 'his heart sins.'
  2:283/q36/p2 Āthim is an advanced predicate and qalbuhu a delayed subject. — reasons: Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa offer this; Samin notes a Kufan objection to a pronoun pointing to the later noun.
  2:283/q36/p3 Qalbuhu is partitive apposition to the pronoun or to the hidden subject. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya proposes apposition; Basrans object to an unsupported active-participle government in one version, while Farra and Akhfash allow it.
  2:283/q36/p4 An intensive explanation makes qalb an accusative specification. — reasons: Abu Hatim proposes an analogy, but Nahhas rejects it because qalbuhu is definite.
2:283/q37 What variant forms of 'his heart is sinful' are read? [ءَاثِمٌۭ قَلْبُهُۥ · readings] (turns on: Whether the heart is nominative, accusative, or object of a finite verb.)
  2:283/q37/p1 Qalbahu in the accusative. — reasons: Ibn Abi Abla's variant is parsed as apposition, object-like accusative or specification. Makki weakens tamyiz because the noun is definite; Basrans object, Kufans adduce 2:130 and 28:85; Sibawayh allows object-like usage in poetry only.
  2:283/q37/p2 Athama or āthama qalbahu, 'he made his heart sinful.' — reasons: Ibrahim ibn Abi Aylah and Ibn Abi Abla transmit a verbal reading, with the heart as object or as whole-person metonymy.
2:283/q38 To whom does the pronoun in 'indeed he' refer? [فَإِنَّهُۥٓ · referent] (turns on: Whether the pronoun resumes 'whoever' or is impersonal with an explanatory clause.)
  2:283/q38/p1 It refers to the person who conceals testimony. — reasons: Samin considers this apparent, and Alusi says most natural.
  2:283/q38/p2 It is a pronoun of the matter explained by what follows. — reasons: Samin and Alusi report the option but note a grammatical objection: the following participial phrase is not a full explanatory sentence under dominant Basran and Kufan rules.
